Since, therefore, this is sure and steadfast, that no other God or Lord was announced by the Spirit, except Him who, as God, rules over all, together with His Word, and those who receive the Spirit of adoption, that is, those who believe in the one and true God, and in Jesus Christ the Son of God;
translator: Alexander Roberts and William Rambaut (Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1, rev. for New Advent by Kevin Knight) - ANF English, excerpt as printed (exact)

what_it_says: Irenaeus says no other God or Lord is proclaimed by the Spirit except the one who rules over all, with His Word, and those who receive the Spirit of adoption, i.e. those who believe in the one true God and in Christ Jesus the Son of God.
use: Supports a Trinitarian reading only in the sense that God is announced together with His Word and with the Spirit; it is not a Trinitarian formula and does not say the Spirit is God.
limits: Anti-Gnostic and anti-Marcionite: the point is the unity of the Creator-God. Opponents (Arians, Unitarians) will read it as a bare monotheism with the Son and Spirit as instruments; the sentence does not settle their status.

english: 2. Now to whom is it not clear, that if the Lord had known many fathers and gods, He would not have taught His disciples to know [only] one God, John 17:3 and to call Him alone Father? But He did the rather distinguish those who by word merely (verbo tenus) are termed gods, from Him who is truly God, that they should not err as to His doctrine, nor understand one [in mistake] for another.
translator: Alexander Roberts and William Rambaut (Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1, rev. for New Advent by Kevin Knight) - ANF English, excerpt as printed (exact)
page: Harvey 1857 vol. 2, p. 146; ANF vol. 1 page unknown
edition: Sancti Irenaei episcopi Lugdunensis libros quinque adversus haereses, ed. W. W. Harvey, vol. 2, Cantabrigiae: Typis Academicis, 1857 (archive.org sanctiirenaeiep00harvgoog); Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (Buffalo: Christian Literature Publishing Co., 1885), as on newadvent.org
what_it_says: Christ's own words (Jn 17:3; Mt 11:25) show that He taught one God and one Father; the 'gods' and 'fathers' of others are so only verbo tenus.
use: Objection-side material: 'one God, one Father' is the Unitarian text. Answer: Irenaeus's point is the contrast between the one true God and beings called gods only by name; it does not deny the Son's divinity, which he affirms elsewhere (Haer. 3-4).
limits: The sentence is about Christ's teaching against false gods; it does not address the Son's relation to the Father. Harvey's variant notes (footnote on 'verbo tenus') not checked in full.

translator: Alexander Roberts and William Rambaut (Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1, rev. for New Advent by Kevin Knight) - ANF English, excerpt as printed (exact)

what_it_says: Irenaeus introduces a quoted saying ('Bene, qui dixit', 'well spoke he who said') that the unmeasurable Father was 'measured' in the Son, the Son being the measure of the Father because He comprehends (capit) Him.
use: Objection (Arian/Unitarian reading: 'measure' = limit, so the Son is bounded and smaller than the Father). Answer from this text alone: the Latin says the Son comprehends/contains the Father, a claim about the Son's relation to the Father that Irenaeus states without saying the Son is a lesser being; the quoted author is not named in the Latin, so the claim cannot be pinned to a source here.
limits: The 'measure' sentence is not the Greek fragment: the Greek printed above the Latin ('Apanta metro kai taxei ho Theos poiei, kai ouden ametron par' autoi, hoti meden anarithmeton', Wisdom 11:21 parallel) is attributed by Harvey's margin to John of Damascus (Parallela) and covers only the first Latin sentence. Harvey's margin 'MASS. IV. xii. 2.' beside the Greek does not match ANF 4.4.2 and is flagged for the Massuet/ANF concordance. Greek of the Son-as-measure sentence not found in the sources read.

translator: Alexander Roberts and William Rambaut (Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1, rev. for New Advent by Kevin Knight) - ANF English, excerpt as printed (exact)
page: Harvey 1857 vol. 2, p. 158; ANF vol. 1 page unknown
edition: Sancti Irenaei episcopi Lugdunensis libros quinque adversus haereses, ed. W. W. Harvey, vol. 2, Cantabrigiae: Typis Academicis, 1857 (archive.org sanctiirenaeiep00harvgoog); Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (Buffalo: Christian Literature Publishing Co., 1885), as on newadvent.org
what_it_says: The Lord, who is the Word, reveals the Father; the Jews who claim to know God reject the Word; 'No man knows the Son but the Father' and vice versa, and he to whom the Son wills to reveal.
use: Answer to the Mt 11:27 / Lk 10:22 objection: the Father is known only through the Son (the Word), so Mt 11:27 does not make the Father unknown before Christ.
limits: Irenaeus is refuting Marcion/Gnostic readings. The 'no one knows the Son but the Father' clause is used by Arians to argue that the Son's knowledge is limited; Irenaeus here uses it for revelation, not for ignorance. Scholarly treatments (Behr, Briggman, Steenberg) not consulted; any reading of them is UNVERIFIED.

what_it_says: If the Son began to exist only at the incarnation, the Father would have been negligent until Tiberius; Irenaeus rejects that the Word was not always with creation, and insists the Son and the Father are to be loved in the same faith.
use: Argues from the eternity of the Word (the Son coexisted with the plasma/creature) against a late-beginning Christ: a Logos-eternity argument usable against Arian 'there was when he was not'.
limits: Irenaeus does not use the word 'eternal generation' here; the sentence is polemical. The Latin 'non semper Verbum ejus una cum plasmate fuisse' is his view that the Word was with the creature from the beginning, not an explicit doctrine of pre-existent generation.

Et Patrem quidem invisibilem et indeterminabilem, quantum ad nos est, cognoscit suum ipsius Verbum, et cum sit inenarrabilis, ipse enarrat eum nobis: rursum autem Verbum suum solus cognoscit Pater.

english: For no one can know the Father, unless through the Word of God, that is, unless by the Son revealing [Him]; neither can he have knowledge of the Son, unless through the good pleasure of the Father.
translator: Alexander Roberts and William Rambaut (Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1, rev. for New Advent by Kevin Knight) - ANF English, excerpt as printed (exact)
page: Harvey 1857 vol. 2, p. 159; ANF vol. 1 page unknown
edition: Sancti Irenaei episcopi Lugdunensis libros quinque adversus haereses, ed. W. W. Harvey, vol. 2, Cantabrigiae: Typis Academicis, 1857 (archive.org sanctiirenaeiep00harvgoog); Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (Buffalo: Christian Literature Publishing Co., 1885), as on newadvent.org
what_it_says: No one knows the Father except through the Word, and the Son is known only by the Father's good pleasure; the Father sends, the Son is sent and comes; the Father is invisible and ineffable 'as far as regards us', the Word alone knows the Father fully and the Father alone knows the Word.
use: Supports a Trinitarian reading (mutual knowledge of Father and Son; the Son does the Father's good pleasure; 'the Father alone knows His own Word'). Also a 'missio' (sending) structure.
limits: Opponents read 'the Son is sent' and 'the Father alone knows the Word' as subordination (Arian/Unitarian). The text is about revelation to us ('quantum ad nos est'), and Irenaeus does not contrast essences. Harvey's footnotes record manuscript variants at 'indeterminabilem' (not checked in detail).

page: Harvey 1857 vol. 2, p. 161; ANF vol. 1 page unknown
edition: Sancti Irenaei episcopi Lugdunensis libros quinque adversus haereses, ed. W. W. Harvey, vol. 2, Cantabrigiae: Typis Academicis, 1857 (archive.org sanctiirenaeiep00harvgoog); Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (Buffalo: Christian Literature Publishing Co., 1885), as on newadvent.org
what_it_says: Through the visible Word the Father was shown; all saw the Father in the Son, 'for the Father is the invisible of the Son, but the Son the visible of the Father', and all who saw Christ called Him God.
use: This is the key visibility sentence. Supports a Trinitarian reading in one direction: the Son is the visible of the Father and the Father is seen in the Son (John 14:9 logic). It also shows the Son is called God by all present.
limits: Objection: 'the Father is the invisible of the Son' suggests the Son sees what the Father does not, i.e. an ordering of knowledge; Arians use the 'visible' contrast to argue the Son is a created image. Irenaeus is not explicit about co-eternity here. The Latin is a 3rd-4th c. translation; the Greek behind 'visibile' and 'invisibile' is not in the Latin text. Harvey's footnote 8 (p. 160) gives Greek 'τὸ ἀόρατον γὰρ τοῦ Υἱοῦ Πατήρ, τὸ δὲ ὁρατὸν τοῦ Πατρὸς Υἱός' with NO source named in the note: treat it as Harvey's reconstruction, not a verified fragment. use: Supports a Trinitarian reading: the Son is 'very God' attested by the Father and the Spirit, and 'the Father making all things subject to Him' is the economic order; the unity of the one who speaks and the one who is known.

ref: 4.7.4 (ANF division; Harvey LIB. IV CAP. XIV §1, p. 164; note 8 on the scan)
greek: Hee enim Filius qui est Verbum Dei ab initio praestruebat, non indigente Patre angelis, uti faceret conditionem et formaret hominem, propter quem et conditio fiebat: neque rursus indigente ministerio ad fabricationem eorum quae facta sunt, ad dispositionem eorum negotiorum, quae secundum hominem erant; sed habente copiosum et inenarrabile ministerium. Ministrat enim ei ad omnia sua progenies et figuratio sua, id est Filius, et Spiritus sanctus, Verbum et Sapientia; quibus serviunt et subjecti sunt omnes angeli.
greek_edition: Latin (no Greek original survives for this sentence in Haer. 4; Latin is the original text here). Harvey 1857 vol. 2, p. 164 (PDF p. 175; Harvey CAP. XIV §1 (p. 164, PDF p. 175); Harvey note 8: 'figuratio, i.e. the Holy Spirit'). english: For His offspring and His similitude do minister to Him in every respect; that is, the Son and the Holy Spirit, the Word and Wisdom; whom all the angels serve, and to whom they are subject.
translator: Alexander Roberts and William Rambaut (Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1, rev. for New Advent by Kevin Knight) - ANF English, excerpt as printed (exact)
page: Harvey 1857 vol. 2, p. 164; ANF vol. 1 page unknown
edition: Sancti Irenaei episcopi Lugdunensis libros quinque adversus haereses, ed. W. W. Harvey, vol. 2, Cantabrigiae: Typis Academicis, 1857 (archive.org sanctiirenaeiep00harvgoog); Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (Buffalo: Christian Literature Publishing Co., 1885), as on newadvent.org
what_it_says: The Father needs no angelic ministry: the Word, and His progenies and figuratio (Son and Holy Spirit, Word and Wisdom), minister to Him, and all angels serve them.
use: A Wisdom/Spirit text: Son and Spirit are both 'Word and Wisdom' and serve the Father, and the Spirit is grouped with the Son as the Father's ministry. Supports a Trinitarian reading only if the Spirit's status is read into this passage; Irenaeus lists the Spirit with the Son as the Father's ministry and does not spell out the Spirit's divinity here.
limits: NEGATIVE CHECK: the brief's description ('the Word and the Spirit ... the Father's hands') does NOT match 4.7.4. ANF 4.7 has no 'hand(s)'; the Latin of Harvey XII-XIV (pdf 173-175) has no 'manus'. The 'hands' texts found in Book IV are the Preface (Latin 'per manus ejus plasmatus est, hoc est, per Filium et Spiritum sanctum', Harvey 1857 vol. 2 Preface, ANF 4.Pr.3) and 4.20.1 (outside this assignment). Subordination objection: 'subjecti sunt omnes angeli' with the Son and Spirit as 'serving' is used by Arians/Unitarians to argue the Son and Spirit are servants.

english: If, therefore, the self-same person is present who was announced by the prophets, our Lord Jesus Christ, and if His advent has brought in a fuller [measure of] grace and greater gifts to those who have received Him, it is plain that the Father also is Himself the same who was proclaimed by the prophets, and that the Son, on His coming, did not spread the knowledge of another Father, but of the same who was preached from the beginning
translator: Alexander Roberts and William Rambaut (Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1, rev. for New Advent by Kevin Knight) - ANF English, excerpt as printed (exact)
page: Harvey 1857 vol. 2, p. 176; ANF vol. 1 page unknown
edition: Sancti Irenaei episcopi Lugdunensis libros quinque adversus haereses, ed. W. W. Harvey, vol. 2, Cantabrigiae: Typis Academicis, 1857 (archive.org sanctiirenaeiep00harvgoog); Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (Buffalo: Christian Literature Publishing Co., 1885), as on newadvent.org
what_it_says: If the Christ present is the one the prophets announced, then the Father is the same one the prophets proclaimed; the Son did not bring knowledge of another Father.
use: Continuity argument: the Father of the prophets is the Father of Christ. Useful against Marcionite two-God readings; supports a unified 'one God, Father, Word' reading.
limits: Says nothing about the Son's consubstantiality. The bracketed 'measure of' in ANF is the translator's, not Irenaeus's (Latin: 'pleniorem gratiam'). Not a 'measure' text despite the brief's grouping.

english: In the beginning, therefore, did God form Adam, not as if He stood in need of man, but that He might have [some one] upon whom to confer His benefits. For not alone antecedently to Adam, but also before all creation, the Word glorified His Father, remaining in Him; and was Himself glorified by the Father,
translator: Alexander Roberts and William Rambaut (Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1, rev. for New Advent by Kevin Knight) - ANF English, excerpt as printed (exact)
page: Harvey 1857 vol. 2, p. 184; ANF vol. 1 page unknown
edition: Sancti Irenaei episcopi Lugdunensis libros quinque adversus haereses, ed. W. W. Harvey, vol. 2, Cantabrigiae: Typis Academicis, 1857 (archive.org sanctiirenaeiep00harvgoog); Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (Buffalo: Christian Literature Publishing Co., 1885), as on newadvent.org
what_it_says: God formed Adam not because He needed man but to confer benefits; before all creation the Word glorified the Father, remaining in Him, and was glorified by the Father.
use: Supports a Trinitarian reading of mutual glorification and the Word's eternal presence in the Father before creation ('before all creation ... remaining in Him').
limits: The 'before all creation' clause is Irenaeus's, but the Latin does not use the term 'eternal'; Arians read 'glorified by the Father' as a derived glory. The ANF 'antecedently' is ANF's rendering of 'ante'.

ref: 4.14.2 (ANF division; Harvey LIB. IV xxv §2, p. 185)
greek: Sic et Deus ab initio hominem quidem plasmavit propter suam munificentiam; patriarchas vero elegit propter illorum salutem; populum vero praeformabat, docens indocibilem sequi Deum; prophetas vero praestruebat in terra, assuescens hominem portare ejus Spiritum, et communionem habere cum Deo: ipse quidem nullius indigens; his vero qui indigent ejus, suam praebens communionem.

english: Thus it was, too, that God formed man at the first, because of His munificence; but chose the patriarchs for the sake of their salvation;
translator: Alexander Roberts and William Rambaut (Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1, rev. for New Advent by Kevin Knight) - ANF English, excerpt as printed (exact)
page: Harvey 1857 vol. 2, p. 185; ANF vol. 1 page unknown
edition: Sancti Irenaei episcopi Lugdunensis libros quinque adversus haereses, ed. W. W. Harvey, vol. 2, Cantabrigiae: Typis Academicis, 1857 (archive.org sanctiirenaeiep00harvgoog); Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (Buffalo: Christian Literature Publishing Co., 1885), as on newadvent.org
what_it_says: God formed man for His bounty, chose the patriarchs for salvation, prepared a people and sent prophets to accustom man to bear God's Spirit and have communion with God; God Himself needs nothing.
use: Supports the Spirit's indwelling and communion as the Spirit given to men (Spirit as God's gift), not a Trinitarian formula.
limits: Opponents will note the Father 'needs nothing' and the Spirit is 'borne' by man, i.e. a creaturely reception. No explicit Triad.

english: Moreover, the prophets indicate in the fullest manner that God stood in no need of their slavish obedience, but that it was upon their own account that He enjoined certain observances in the law.
translator: Alexander Roberts and William Rambaut (Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1, rev. for New Advent by Kevin Knight) - ANF English, excerpt as printed (exact)
page: Harvey 1857 vol. 2, p. 193; ANF vol. 1 page unknown
edition: Sancti Irenaei episcopi Lugdunensis libros quinque adversus haereses, ed. W. W. Harvey, vol. 2, Cantabrigiae: Typis Academicis, 1857 (archive.org sanctiirenaeiep00harvgoog); Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (Buffalo: Christian Literature Publishing Co., 1885), as on newadvent.org
what_it_says: God needs neither the obedience nor the oblation of men; the observances of the law were for men's sake.
use: Not a Trinitarian text. Use only for the 'God is not in need' theme (God's aseity), which supports the classical divine-impassibility/aseity account.
limits: The brief's 4.17 topic is a metaphysics point; it says nothing about the Son or the Spirit. Its Latin and 'Samuel/David' prooftexts are the usual Old Testament argument.

greek: Sed terrena quidem, quae sunt erga nos disposita, congruit typos esse eorum quae sunt coelestia, ab eodem tamen Deo facta. Nec enim aliter poterat assimilare spiritalium imaginem. Quae autem supercoelestia, et spiritalia sunt, et quantum ad nos spectat, invisibilia et inenarrabilia, typos rursus alterorum coelestium dicere, et alterius pleromatis, et Deum alterius patris imaginem esse, et errantium est a veritate.

english: But to allege that those things which are super-celestial and spiritual, and, as far as we are concerned, invisible and ineffable, are in their turn the types of celestial things and of another Pleroma, and [to say] that God is the image of another Father, is to play the part both of wanderers from the truth, and of absolutely foolish and stupid persons.
translator: Alexander Roberts and William Rambaut (Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1, rev. for New Advent by Kevin Knight) - ANF English, excerpt as printed (exact)
page: Harvey 1857 vol. 2, p. 210; ANF vol. 1 page unknown
edition: Sancti Irenaei episcopi Lugdunensis libros quinque adversus haereses, ed. W. W. Harvey, vol. 2, Cantabrigiae: Typis Academicis, 1857 (archive.org sanctiirenaeiep00harvgoog); Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (Buffalo: Christian Literature Publishing Co., 1885), as on newadvent.org
what_it_says: Earthly things are types of heavenly things, all made by the one God; but to say the super-celestial, invisible and ineffable things are types of another Pleroma, or God the image of another Father, is error.
use: Against Gnostic 'types of types' and 'another Father': supports the reading of the Father as one invisible and ineffable God, the same God who made the visible world.
limits: Not a Son/Spirit text. Anti-Valentinian; nothing about the generation of the Son (see brief item 3 for that).

greek: Quatenus super Deum extollitis cogitationes vestras, inconsiderate elati? Audistis mensos esse coelos in palma; dicite mihi mensuram, et enarrate multitudinem cubitorum innumerabilem, exponite mihi plenitudinem, latitudinem, et longitudinem, et altitudinem, circummensurationis initium et finem, quae non intelligit cor hominis, et non comprehendit ea. Vere enim magna sunt thesaurophylacia coelestia: immensurabilis est in corde Deus, et incomprehensibilis in animo, qui comprehendit terram pugillo. Quis respicit mensuram dextrae ejus? Digitum quis cognoscit?

english: To these persons one may with justice say (as Scripture itself suggests), To what distance above God do you lift up your imaginations, O you rashly elated men? You have heard that the heavens are meted out in the palm of [His] hand: Isaiah 40:12 tell me the measure, and recount the endless multitude of cubits, explain to me the fullness, the breadth, the length, the height, the beginning and end of the measurement — things which the heart of man understands not, neither does it comprehend them. For the heavenly treasuries are indeed great: God cannot be measured in the heart, and incomprehensible is He in the mind; He who holds the earth in the hollow of His hand. Who perceives the measure of His right hand? Who knows His finger?
translator: Alexander Roberts and William Rambaut (Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1, rev. for New Advent by Kevin Knight) - ANF English, excerpt as printed (exact)
page: Harvey 1857 vol. 2, p. 211; ANF vol. 1 page unknown
edition: Sancti Irenaei episcopi Lugdunensis libros quinque adversus haereses, ed. W. W. Harvey, vol. 2, Cantabrigiae: Typis Academicis, 1857 (archive.org sanctiirenaeiep00harvgoog); Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (Buffalo: Christian Literature Publishing Co., 1885), as on newadvent.org
what_it_says: Scripture says God measures the heavens in His palm (Is 40:12); no one can measure God in the heart, and God is incomprehensible; His hand, which measures immensity, holds the earth.
use: Supports divine incomprehensibility and immensity ('immensurabilis est in corde Deus'). The 'hand' imagery is the Father's hand with Word and Spirit in Haer. 4.20, not here.
limits: Measure/limit language: 'mensura' here is a 'measure' held by the Father's hand, not a 'measure' of the Son. Do not conflate with 4.4.2 ('the Son is the measure of the Father'), where the Latin is 'mensura enim Patris Filius'. Opening word uncertain in OCR.
